target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers and help the people most constrained by work
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off or even a day off from private employers, especially in retail and service jobs, so low-income workers could still be scheduled to work, lose wages, or face attendance penalties. Because the workers with the tightest schedules may still have to work, the holiday would not reliably remove the main barrier to voting for them.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday by itself is an effective way to increase turnout
objection: Even if a holiday makes voting more convenient for some people, calendar changes alone are not a reliable turnout strategy; turnout is more strongly improved by reforms that directly reduce logistical and administrative friction, such as guaranteed time to vote, easier registration, and accessible voting methods.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday leaves the biggest scheduling barriers largely intact for low-income workers
objection: That objection assumes a holiday is only a symbolic calendar label. In practice, a national holiday changes scheduling norms: government offices and schools close, and many private employers reduce staffing or adjust hours. That means the lost-wages and inflexible-shift barrier is not left largely intact, because many workers would have more actual free time to vote.

target: AG1's original claim that a national holiday directly removes practical scheduling barriers for most voters
objection: A federal holiday changes the calendar but does not require private employers to give paid time off or close. As a result, many low-income retail and service workers can still be forced to work or take unpaid time, so the main real-world costs of voting remain for those voters.

target: AG1's broader claim that a holiday meaningfully reduces barriers for the voters most constrained by work and school
objection: Even if a holiday helps some people, Election Day as a holiday is not a dependable turnout increase. Reforms that directly guarantee time to vote and reduce administrative friction are more effective than a holiday alone.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday mostly leaves the biggest costs intact because private employers are not legally required to provide paid time off
objection: The objection overstates how little a holiday changes. Federal holidays typically trigger widespread shutdowns or holiday scheduling norms in schools, offices, and many private workplaces, so the policy meaningfully reduces the need for workers to miss wages or risk penalties in order to vote, even if not every employer is legally required to provide paid leave.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday is the better solution to voting barriers than targeted reforms
objection: A holiday would not reliably solve the main voting barrier for low-income workers because it does not ensure paid time off or freedom from scheduling conflict in the workplaces where those voters are concentrated. More targeted reforms, such as state rules requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration, more directly address the problem.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday does not meaningfully help low-income workers because private employers need not provide paid time off
objection: The key barrier is not just whether every employer provides paid leave; it is that normal weekday work and school routines make voting hard to fit into the available hours. A national holiday changes those routines at the system level by closing schools and shifting many businesses to holiday schedules, which reduces scheduling friction and helps low-income workers as well.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday changes routines broadly enough to help low-income workers
objection: Even if schools close, many low-income workers are employed by retailers, restaurants, and other service businesses that remain open and staff shifts on federal holidays. Because those workers can still face lost wages, scheduling conflicts, or discipline for missing work, the claimed mechanism does not reliably reduce the core tradeoff between voting and keeping a job.

target: AG2's broader argument that a national holiday would not reliably reduce constraints for low-income voters
objection: A national holiday does change day-to-day routines broadly: schools close or run on holiday schedules, and many workplaces do too. That reduces the need to request time off, arrange childcare, or miss class, and it can help the least flexible workers by easing the calendar-based constraints that block voting.

target: AG1's assumption that a national holiday reliably changes work routines enough to reduce scheduling constraints for low-income workers
objection: The claimed mechanism is unreliable because the workers most affected are disproportionately in retail and service jobs, and holiday status does not force those employers to close or provide paid time to vote. Many low-income workers would still have shifts during voting hours and still face wage loss or conflict with work, so the holiday does not reliably reduce their practical constraints.
